title: Normal/inverse sandwich structure series-engineered multilayer double-atom catalysts featuring bridge-bonded dual-sulfur ligands: Machine learning-driven optimization for oxygen evolution/reduction reaction bifunctional electrocatalysts
abstract: Although a graphene-like carbon nitride monolayer (N4@g-C16N3) supported transition metal (TM) has been confirmed to possess excellent oxygen evolution/reduction reaction (OER/ORR) activity, we believe that certain modulation strategies can release significant potential for further enhancement. As such, we explored the potential of multilayer normal/inverse sandwich structures series derived from N4@g-C16N3 with dual-sulfur bridging for OER/ORR applications using density functional theory (DFT) and machine learning (ML). Initially, by comparing 27 double-atom catalysts (TMN4-S2-TMN4) dwelled in bilayer homonuclear normal sandwich structures with 27 single-atom catalysts ((TM-N4)@g-C16N3), confirming increased activities in bilayer systems and six high-activity TM-atoms stand out, leading to the generation of 183 bilayer normal/inverse sandwich structures. Orbital population analysis revealed that altering active metal atoms to synergize with dual-sulfur bridging layers can significantly impact bond order to optimize adsorption free energy (ΔGO*), a key descriptor for OER/ORR overpotentials. Subsequently, we employed an update bond order scheme to describe O* adsorption strength, introducing bond order corrections by analyzing bonding/antibonding electrons correlation with ΔGO*, thereby enhancing the scheme’s capability to describe OER/ORR activity and further explaining its origins. Under this framework, FeN4-S2-AgN4 exhibits the most suitable metal-O* interaction, demonstrated by excellent bifunctional performance. Based on 181 bilayer structures, we performed ML predictions on 548 others and validated the results using DFT. Additionally, constant-potential simulations reveal that the electric double layer plays a regulatory role in modulating reaction barriers, while the adsorption free energies, governed by both pH and electrode potential, underscore the excellent OER/ORR catalytic performance across a wide pH spectrum. By constructing simplified structural descriptors (φ), we labeled microenvironment changes around active sites caused by varying layer numbers and metal combinations, improving model’s generalizability and extended predictions for OER/ORR overpotentials to pseudo-bilayer and bi/tri/quadlayer sandwich systems (2,916 configurations), validated by DFT calculations. Meanwhile, formation energy predictions guarantee that these structures possess high thermal stability, supporting their practical feasibility.

title: Inverse ligand design: a generative data-driven model for optimizing vanadyl-based epoxidation catalysts
abstract: We present a machine learning (ML) model for the inverse, de novo generative design of vanadyl-based catalyst ligands for the epoxidation of small alkenes and alcohols. Leveraging molecular descriptors calculated using the RDKit library, our model achieves high performance in validity (64.7 %), uniqueness (89.6 %), and RDKit similarity (91.8 %) after training on a curated dataset of six million structures. Focusing on the modular nature of vanadyl catalyst scaffolds – VOSO 4 , VO(O i Pr) 3 and VO(acac) 2 – the model generates feasible ligands optimized for catalytic performance. The VOSO 4 ligands were consistent with high-yield reactions, while VO(O i Pr) 3 and VO(acac) 2 revealed greater structure variability. Unlike conventional generative approaches, the ligand inverse design also aims to co-design the reaction system, including substrate SMILES and reaction conditions. The model framework was investigated using multiple generative model architectures, resulting in the deep-learning transformer as the most powerful, and uncovering clustering patterns in electronic and structural descriptors related to yield predictions. High synthetic accessibility scores supported the feasibility of the generated ligands. Although the experimental dataset lacks modularity and has few negative data, the model compensates this by using structured descriptor encoding and compatibility scoring. This generative ML framework shows a scalable approach to catalyst ligand design, paving the way for efficient data optimization in synthetic chemistry.

title: Mobility and sintering of silica-supported platinum clusters via reactive neural network potentials
abstract: Supported Pt atoms and their sub-nanometre cluster counterparts are a promising avenue for the targeted, bottom-up development of high specific activity heterogeneous catalysts. However, they suffer from instability with respect to growth and deactivation via sintering. The atomistic processes which comprise the early stages of sintering are difficult to access, as the timescales are too long for traditional electronic structure calculation methods and too short for most experimental techniques to probe. Pinning via hydroxyl groups has been suggested as a means to stabilize small clusters, but the means and extent of this sintering resistance is currently unclear. In this work, neural network potentials (NNPs), trained at the dispersion-corrected metaGGA level of theory, are employed to probe the dynamic behaviour of sub-nanometre Ptx species (x = 1, 3, 15) on a model flat oxide support: silicatene. We observe that mobility is surprisingly lowest for the single Pt atom and highest for the larger cluster, which influences the sintering routes, leading to non-Ostwald ripening coalescence pathways. When a silanol defect is introduced to the surface, the clusters are stabilised by the defect via hydrogen transfer from the surface to the clusters, thereby suppressing sintering via electrostatic trapping. These findings provide a mechanistic underpinning of sintering routes and stabilisation mechanisms on a model non-reducible oxide support and provide insights into the mechanisms of sub-nanometre metal particle mobility at the atomistic scale.

title: Machine learning–assisted discovery of chromium bis(2-pyridyl)amine catalysts for ethylene tri-/tetramerization
abstract: The selective production of 1-hexene and 1-octene through chromium-catalyzed ethylene oligomerization remains a central challenge in catalyst design. In this work, we developed a fully automated, data-driven workflow to investigate the chromium bis(2-pyridyl)amine (Cr/NNN) catalytic system. A virtual database of 256 ligands with systematically varied R1-R3 substituents was constructed, and the relative transition-state Gibbs free energy differences (ΔΔG) between trimerization and tetramerization pathways were computed using DFT. To efficiently represent the key structural and physicochemical characteristics of the catalysts, molecular descriptors were extracted using SMILES-based structure generation combined with xTB calculations and RDKit-derived structural analysis. The developed machine learning models exhibited excellent predictive performance, achieving an R2 of 0.90 and a remarkably low MAE of 0.52 kcal/mol. Subsequent SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified the key structural features governing ΔΔG, confirming that the selectivity is primarily controlled by local steric effects at R1, with distant electronic substitutions contributing only weakly. Guided by the machine learning and SHAP analyses, two Cr/NNN catalysts were identified from the DFT-calculated dataset as optimal prototypes, showing exclusive selectivity for 1-hexene and 1-octene formation, respectively. This data-driven strategy can be readily extended to other transition-metal catalytic systems, offering a general framework for accelerating catalyst discovery and selectivity optimization.

title: The influence of the organic residue and the solvent in the Schlenk equilibrium for Grignard reagents in THF. A molecular dynamics study with machine learning potentials
abstract: The Schlenk equilibrium is an essential characteristic of the Grignard reagents. However, its quantitative aspects remain poorly understood. In this work, we perform molecular dynamics simulations to characterise how the Schlenk reaction is affected by varying the alkyl R groups (Me, Et, i -Pr, t -Bu). For each R group, the reactivity profiles were obtained through enhanced sampling on fully solvated dinuclear species, leveraging a newly developed machine learning potential trained on ab initio data. While the topologies of the Helmholtz energy maps are qualitatively similar, the energy ranges vary significantly with the R groups. Bulkier R groups disfavour higher solvation of the magnesium centre, with direct implications for the activation and mechanism of the Schlenk exchange. With respect to dichloro-bridged species, the concentrations of monochloro-bridged and separated species increase with the size of R and the degree of solvation. The energy barrier for ligand exchange increases with the size of R, and it is particularly noticeable for R = t -Bu, in agreement with experimental data. As excess solvation of one of the magnesium centres is associated with the most important reaction pathways, it can be deduced that early formation of monochloro-bridged species favours the Cl/R exchange, especially for large R groups. The formation of these species is favoured by higher Mg solvation for small R groups, and by the steric volume of R itself for large R, pointing at a constructive effect of the solvent and R promoting Cl/R exchange. Our study shows that a full characterisation of the speciation of Grignard reagents in solution is possible at reasonable computational costs with machine-learning potentials.

title: Protonation dynamics of confined ethanol–water mixtures in H-ZSM-5 from machine learning-driven metadynamics
abstract: Zeolites are indispensable heterogeneous catalysts in industrial chemical processes, valued for their strong Brønsted acidity, well-defined microporous frameworks, and tunable pore structures. Their catalytic activity arises primarily from Brønsted acid sites (BAS), typically present as bridging hydroxyl groups (Si–OH–Al). Under aqueous reaction conditions, these protons interact dynamically with water and alcohol molecules, leading to complex solvation and protonation behavior within confined pores. In this study, we investigate the protonation equilibrium occurring between ethanol and water at the BAS of acidic zeolites under varying hydration levels, i.e., C2H5OH–(H2O)n, n=1–4. Local structure was analyzed through an adaptive-learning global optimization algorithm, while enhanced sampling molecular dynamics simulations with Well-Tempered Metadynamics (WMetaD) and machine learning interatomic potentials (MLPs) provide free-energy surfaces (FES) at variable hydration levels. The results reveal a strong dependence of proton localization on the degree of hydration. At low hydration (1 water molecule), the proton resides predominantly on ethanol; with 2 water molecules, it shifts toward water, and at higher hydration (3 or more water molecules), it becomes extensively delocalized over the water cluster. These findings underscore the critical role of solvation in modulating acid site behavior and suggest that a minimum of three water molecules is necessary to fully stabilize the proton on water within the zeolite framework. This solvation threshold has significant implications for catalytic processes, particularly in biomass conversion reactions where alcohol protonation is a key step in dehydration mechanisms.

title: Microkinetic modeling of methane activation in Mo/ZSM-5 with machine learning potentials
abstract: Mo/ZSM-5 catalyzes methane dehydroaromatization (MDA), yet the role of entropy on reactive intermediates and transition states remain unresolved. At reaction temperatures of 1000 K, the entropic contributions to the Gibbs free energy of reactive intermediates and transition states are challenging to model and can have consequences for predicting reaction kinetics and steady state coverages. The structure and distribution of active sites during MDA turnovers is complex and here we investigate the simplest ion-exchanged Mo carbide active site in ZSM-5 to isolate how entropy models affect methane activation. We consider two pathways: a C–C coupling pathway that forms ethylene after sequential methane dehydrogenation, and a MoC regeneration pathway that directly forms ethylene then reconstitutes [MoC]2+ sites. The harmonic oscillator approximation and partition function methods that assign hindered translational and rotational motions to low frequency modes were used to compute entropies at 1000 K. We then applied molecular dynamics using a machine learned potential (MLP) to obtain activation free energies for methane activation and hydrogen association via well-tempered metadynamics. Monte Carlo integration using an MLP was used to explicitly calculate translational and rotational entropy contributions for adsorbed methane. By comparing different entropy models, we demonstrate that translational and rotational modes are necessary for weakly adsorbed intermediates. Mean-field microkinetic modeling was used to quantify reaction orders and apparent activation energies for different entropy approximations. On this mononuclear MoC site, C–C coupling of unsaturated carbon intermediates is kinetically favored for direct ethylene formation, and the apparent kinetics depend on the entropy model. This manuscript demonstrates how MLPs in conjunction with enhanced sampling and Monte Carlo integration can inform entropy approaches in a reaction network to be integrated into microkinetic models.

title: Integrating DFT and machine learning for a dual-descriptor strategy in Gold(I) catalyst design: π-bond activation and orbital interactions
abstract: Interpretable understanding of ligand effects remains a key challenge in homogeneous gold(I) catalysis, particularly for reactions in which experimentally optimized systems already display high performance. Here, we combine density functional theory and interpretable machine learning (ML) to map ligand effects in Au(I)-catalyzed [2 + 2] cycloadditions of aryl alkynes and alkenes. A diverse set of 100 phosphine ligands was evaluated by DFT, and ensemble ML models trained on physically motivated descriptors reveal clear structure–reactivity relationships. The analysis consistently identifies the experimentally employed ligand as residing within the near-optimal region of the predicted activity–selectivity landscape, with closely related ligands occupying progressively less favorable regions. Targeted experimental comparisons and additional DFT calculations on representative ligands confirm these predicted trends and show that ligand variation does not induce a turnover-limiting step shift within the explored chemical space. These results provide an experimentally supported mapping of attainable ligand effects and intrinsic performance boundaries in this Au(I)-catalyzed system, highlighting the value of boundary-aware, interpretable machine learning approaches for understanding established gold catalysis.

title: Robust extraction of thermodynamically consistent neural-network-based kinetic models from reactor data: Methanation, methanol synthesis, and dimethyl ether synthesis
abstract: Kinetic models are central to the design, analysis, and control of catalytic reaction systems. Current kinetic modeling approaches rely on mechanistic rate expressions derived and parameterized using chemical intuition, ab initio calculations, and laboratory reactor measurements. However, this process is time-intensive and requires substantial system-specific expert knowledge. These challenges motivate the development of alternative frameworks to efficiently extract kinetic models directly from experimental reactor datasets. Here, we demonstrate robust extraction of stoichiometrically and thermodynamically consistent neural-network-based kinetic models from laboratory reactor data for three industrially relevant catalytic systems: methanation, methanol synthesis, and dimethyl ether synthesis. We first identify failure modes that hinder training and then introduce a bounded Global Reaction Neural Network architecture (\pmGRNN) that limits the contribution of the thermodynamic driving force to enable stable optimization. Using this architecture, we extract accurate kinetic models for all three systems that generalize to previously unseen operating conditions. For dimethyl ether synthesis over a mixed-catalyst system, the framework correctly attributes methanol synthesis to the CuO/ZnO/Al 2 O 3 catalyst and methanol dehydration to the γ-Al 2 O 3 catalyst without imposing a priori reaction-catalyst assignments. Taken together, these results support neural-network-based kinetic model extraction as a practical route to efficiently derive physically consistent kinetics from reactor data across catalytic reaction systems.

title: Isobutanol dehydration catalyzed by bridging OH groups at the (100) surface of ferrierite: From static DFT to machine learning accelerated molecular dynamics
abstract: Ferrierite is industrially used as a catalyst for the dehydration of isobutanol into butenes and the critical part of this transformation is presumably catalyzed by Brønsted acid (BA) sites located on its external surface. In this work, we present a DFT investigation of a complete reaction network over the T1O3 BA site at the (100) surface of this zeolite. Exploration of reaction mechanisms by means of the static approach revealed that the transformation towards all products proceeds in two steps - dehydration and deprotonation - with the former step being rate determining for all competing reaction channels. Free energetics of the dehydration reaction was therefore investigated using ab initio molecular dynamics accelerated by machine-learned force fields with accuracy controlled via a correction scheme based on machine learning perturbation theory. The activation free energies for transformations towards branched and linear products computed using the PBE+D2 functional (111.3 and 125.7 kJ/mol, respectively) suggest a preference of the former reaction channel. This conclusion was found to be independent of the dispersion correction used with the PBE functional (no correction, D3, D3(BJ), and D4) and of the choice of bridging OH group, as shown for the alternative T3O1 and T4O7 sites. Interestingly, our results are in agreement with our previous investigation of analogous reactions catalyzed by bulk chabazite. At the same time, however, they do not reproduce the experimental selectivities observed for ferrierite, which suggests that the bridging OH groups are not at the origin of the specific selectivity of ferrierite for linear alkenes.

title: DFT and machine learning insights into productive versus self-metathesis selectivity in ruthenium-catalyzed ethenolysis
abstract: Ethenolysis, the catalytic cross-metathesis of carbon-carbon double bonds with ethylene, represents an important route for the production of high-value terminal olefins. In this work, density functional theory (DFT) calculations and parallel machine learning (ML) analyses were employed to investigate the factors that alter the reaction selectivity during ruthenium-catalyzed ethenolysis of ethyl oleate. In this context, the selectivity was evaluated as the competition between productive metathesis (PM) and self-metathesis (SM), with the thermodynamic preference for catalyst recovery emerging as the determinant process. In particular, the overall reaction energy associated with PM and, in turn, catalyst regeneration, consistently correlates with experimental selectivity trends. Complementary ML analyses, based on tree-based ensemble algorithms, further demonstrate that catalytic performance arises from multidimensional relationships between various steric and electronic descriptors rather than from isolated electronic properties. These findings establish a predictive framework for the rational design and evaluation of selective ruthenium catalysts for sustainable olefin metathesis applications.

title: Suppressing nanoparticle aggregation via engineered surface separation walls: a machine learning–driven molecular dynamics and experimental study
abstract: Enhancing the thermal stability of supported metal nanoparticles at high temperatures remains a significant challenge. The efficacy of constructing surface separation walls in mitigating nanoparticle aggregation was evaluated through complementary molecular dynamics simulations and experiments. Using machine learning potential, the effects of separation wall sizes including height, width, length and nanoparticle diameters on the aggregation behavior of Fe nanoparticles supported on Al2O3 surfaces were investigated. For separation walls of infinite length, increasing either the height or width consistently suppresses aggregation of Fe nanoparticles of given diameters. However, for walls of finite length, simply increasing the height is not always effective, as nanoparticles can migrate around the ends of walls. In the case of infinitely long walls, the height-to-diameter ratio determines the onset of aggregation. This critical ratio exhibits a negative correlation with the wall width. Finally, experiments clearly demonstrated the effectiveness of separation walls in enhancing Fe nanoparticles’ high-temperature stability. Finally, the simulations and experiments together reveal a system-dependent synergistic stabilization mechanism for Fe/Al2O3, in which geometric confinement by the separation walls and defect-/interface-mediated metal–support interactions act in concert; the critical height-to-diameter ratio derived from the atomistic simulations is intended as a qualitative design guideline rather than a universal quantitative threshold.

title: Activation barriers in the glycolysis of PET as catalyzed by tertiary amines: Density functional calculations and predictions from interpretable machine learning
abstract: The efficient chemical recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a crucial part of any sustainable circular plastic economy. The depolymerization of PET can take place via a glycolysis reaction with tertiary amines as catalysts. We investigate this reaction using density functional calculations with the M06-L functional, complemented by interpretable machine learning. A PET dimer containing C–O linkages is used as a representative model of the active region or the polymer. The concerted and the stepwise mechanisms of its glycolysis using trimethylamine as a catalyst are examined. The calculations reveal that the reaction proceeds preferentially via a stepwise mechanism with which the proton abstraction process being the rate-determining step. The structure–activity relationship shows that, in general, amines with side chains that are better electron donors enhance the reactivity. Deviations from this trend can be attributed to steric hindrance and resonance effects. Based on the analysis of DFT-derived descriptors, the protonation free energy of the tertiary amines is identified as the most important single descriptor for predicting activation barriers. The Sure Independence Screening and Sparsifying Operator (SISSO) method is then employed to develop a few low-dimensional descriptors that enable a reliable prediction of activation barriers based solely on amine properties, thus eliminating the need for the computationally costly explicit transition state calculations.

title: Interpretable machine learning-guided identification of C/H/O affinity descriptors for CO2-to-CH4 electrocatalysis on doped Cu surfaces
abstract: The electroreduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to methane (CH4) over copper (Cu)-based catalysts is a promising route for sustainable fuel production. However, the reaction mechanism remains under debate because competing pathways can proceed through the key *COH and *CHO intermediates. Herein, we constructed 1,331 Cu-based catalyst models containing up to three metal and/or nonmetal dopants and employed CHGNet to rapidly evaluate the energetics of reaction intermediates along the COH and CHO pathways. By correlating key intermediate adsorption energies and the reaction-energy change of the limiting step (ΔElim) with surface C/H/O affinities, we elucidate their distinct roles in CH4 formation. Most doped Cu surfaces exhibit a thermodynamic preference for the CHO pathway over the COH pathway. H-affinity predominantly influences the adsorption energetics of key intermediates, whereas O-affinity strongly affects the limiting reaction-energy requirement for CH4 formation by modulating ΔElim. In the investigated catalyst space, dopants with higher d-electron counts tend to weaken O affinity and thereby reduce ΔElim. In contrast, C-affinity shows a comparatively limited correlation with intermediate adsorption energetics and ΔElim. These findings clarify how surface C/H/O affinities regulate CH4-forming pathways and provide design principles for Cu-based electrocatalysts with favorable CH4 formation energetics.

title: Mechanistic insights and structure–reactivity relationships of Ru(II)–Imidazole complex catalysts for formic acid dehydrogenation: A combined DFT and machine learning study
abstract: Formic acid dehydrogenation is a key reaction for hydrogen storage and release, and understanding its catalytic mechanism and structure–activity relationship is crucial for catalyst design. Here, DFT calculations were combined with machine learning (ML) to investigate ruthenium–imidazole amine complexes for formic acid dehydrogenation. DFT results show that the reaction preferentially occurs through the γ-N proton-responsive site via a stepwise pathway, with β-hydride elimination as the rate-determining step (ΔG≠ = 21.4 kcal/mol, relative to the resting state B-Int2), while the α-N pathway has a higher barrier (ΔG≠ = 33.4 kcal/mol, relative to B-Int2). Distortion/interaction analysis and IGMH analysis reveal that the superior activity of the γ-N pathway mainly originates from lower structural distortion energy and reduced steric repulsion, indicating distortion energy as the dominant factor controlling transition-state stability. Based on DFT data, an ML dataset including different metal centers (Ru, Fe, Os) and ligand substituents was constructed. Among eight regression models, the gradient boosting model showed the best performance (test R2 = 0.808, RMSE = 1.295 kcal/mol). SHAP analysis identified metal charge (qM) as the dominant descriptor, highlighting the importance of electronic effects. Further analysis revealed a volcano-shaped relationship between the HOMO–LUMO energy gap (Egap) and the reaction barrier, identifying an optimal Egap window (≈2.96 eV) where the barrier is minimized, underscoring that balanced electronic modulation is essential for high catalytic performance. These findings provide mechanistic insights into dual-proton-responsive sites and guide the rational design of efficient formic acid dehydrogenation catalysts.
